# Cardiovascular examination

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Basics of cardiology > Cardiovascular examination*

[Original Article Link](/library/rM0fJg)

---

## Summary

The cardiovascular examination is an essential cardiological tool that comprises the assessment of <u>vital signs</u> and <u>jugular venous pulse</u>, <u>chest inspection</u> and palpation, and, most importantly, <u>auscultation of the heart</u>. For specific <u>auscultatory</u> findings in <u>valvular heart disease</u>, see “<u>Auscultation in valvular defects</u>.” For specific <u>auscultatory</u> findings of <u>heart</u> defects, see “<u>Congenital heart defects</u>.” Details regarding the specific signs and symptoms of cardiovascular disease can be found via the links provided below.

---

## History and general examination

### History [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Chest pain</u> (see “<u>Cardiovascular causes of chest pain</u>”)

* Palpitations: an unpleasant awareness of one's own heartbeat; can feel like a fluttering or pounding in the chest

* <u>Syncope</u>

* <u>Hemoptysis</u>

* <u>Edema</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Claudication</u>





### General examination [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




#### Appearance




* <u>Level of consciousness</u>

* Syndromic features (e.g., in <u>trisomy 21</u>, <u>trisomy 18</u>; associated with <u>congenital heart defects</u>)

* Features of <u>rheumatic fever</u>: migrating <u>polyarthritis</u>, <u>erythema marginatum</u>, subcutaneous <u>nodules</u>

* <u>Features of left-sided heart failure</u>

* <u>Features of right-sided heart failure</u>

## Blood pressure

### Approach [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)



1. * The patient should sit for several minutes before blood pressure is measured.
2. * Use the correct cuff size.
3. * Ask the patient to rest the arm on a horizontal surface at the level of the <u>heart</u>.
4. * Record the pressure in both arms and note any differences.
5. * Determine the systolic and <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure value (e.g., <u>auscultatory</u> method using <u>Korotkoff sounds</u> over the <u>brachial artery</u>).
6. * Repeat measurement.




24-hour <u>ambulatory blood pressure measurement</u> can be helpful in establishing the average and peak blood pressure values during daily activities.




### Interpretation




* Korotkoff sounds

* Definition: sounds heard when <u>auscultating</u> over the <u>brachial artery</u> during <u>sphygmomanometry</u>

* Origin: <u>turbulent blood flow</u> through a <u>brachial artery</u> that is partially compressed by the inflated arm cuff of a <u>sphygmomanometer</u>

* Interpretation: When deflating the cuff, the pressure at which <u>Korotkoff sounds</u> appear marks systolic BP, and the pressure at which <u>Korotkoff sounds</u> disappear marks <u>diastolic</u> BP.

* Normal blood pressure

* Systolic blood pressure < 120 mm Hg and <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure < 80 mm Hg [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)

* See also “<u>Normal vital signs at rest</u>” for all age groups.

* Hypotension

* Systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg  [[2]](/library/0YXen9)

* See “<u>Orthostatic syncope</u>.”

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* Systolic blood pressure ≥ 130 mm Hg and/or a <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure ≥ 80 mm Hg  [[3]](/library/OzaIGM)

* See “<u>Diagnosis of hypertension</u>.”





![Blood pressure measurement](media/hkj9ypg4k6ip4yq7jc0qkmpi.jpg)

Blood pressure measurement

![Measuring Blood Pressure - Measuring Vital Signs](media/small_60753e6bd4938.jpg)

Measuring Blood Pressure - Measuring Vital Signs




### Sources of errors in <u>blood pressure measurement</u> [[4]](/library/XYX9n9)




* Incorrect positioning

* <u>White coat hypertension</u>

* Mönckeberg <u>arteriosclerosis</u>  [[5]](/library/cYXaL9)

* Incorrect cuff size

* Auscultatory gap

* <u>Korotkoff sounds</u> between systolic and <u>diastolic</u> blood pressures sometimes diminish or disappear, presumably due to increased arterial stiffness in hypertensive patients.

* When the cuff is insufficiently pumped (i.e., below systolic blood pressure), the first appearance of <u>Korotkoff sounds</u> is misinterpreted as systolic blood pressure (a falsely low reading).

* The falsely low reading can be prevented by simultaneously palpating the radial <u>pulse</u> on the arm in which blood pressure is measured.

## Jugular venous pressure

<u>Jugular venous pressure</u> (<u>JVP</u>) can be used to estimate <u>central venous pressure</u> (<u>CVP</u>) and provides information about fluid status and cardiac function.




### Approach [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* The patient should be in the <u>supine position</u>, torso elevated to 45°, with the head extended backward and turned to the left.

* Identify the venous pulsation of the <u>internal jugular vein</u> and evaluate the following:

* The height of the internal jugular venous filling pressure, by measuring it from the <u>sternal angle</u>

* Estimation of the <u>CVP</u>, obtained by adding 5 cm to the <u>JVP</u> height

* The character of the <u>JVP</u>, by assessing <u>JVP</u> waves

* <u>Hepatojugular reflux</u> should be tested if <u>JVP</u> cannot be assessed properly.





![Examination of the Jugular Venous Pressure - Clinical Examination](media/small_60753cf852e35.jpg)

Examination of the Jugular Venous Pressure - Clinical Examination

![Testing the Hepatojugular Reflux - Clinical Examination](media/small_60753d0e723a2.jpg)

Testing the Hepatojugular Reflux - Clinical Examination




### Interpretation [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




#### Height




* Elevated <u>JVP</u>: > 4 cm filling level of the <u>internal jugular vein</u> above the sternal notch

* Signs of an elevated <u>JVP</u>

* <u>Jugular venous distention</u>

* Kussmaul sign: distention of the jugular <u>veins</u> during inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure that attempts to pull blood into the right <u>heart</u>, which is restricted by noncompliant <u>pericardium</u> or <u>myocardium</u> (e.g., <u>constrictive pericarditis</u>, <u>restrictive cardiomyopathy</u>, right atrial tumors, ventricular tumors, <u>right HF</u>, <u>massive PE</u>)  [[6]](/library/bXXH99)

* <u>Hepatojugular reflux</u>

* Causes of elevated <u>JVP</u>

* <u>Right heart failure</u>

* <u>Fluid overload</u>

* <u>Tricuspid valve</u> dysfunction

* <u>Pericardial effusion</u>

* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u>

* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u>

* <u>SVC syndrome</u>

* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u>





#### Character




A normal <u>JVP</u> waveform consists of three waves (a, c, v) and two descents (x, y).




| <br><u>JVP</u> waves and abnormalities  [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wave | Description | <br>Abnormalities <br> |
| a wave | <br>* The first peak caused by atrial contraction<br><br> | <br>* Absent in <u>atrial fibrillation</u><br><br> |
| c wave | <br>* The second peak caused by <u>tricuspid valve</u> closure, contraction of the <u>right ventricle</u>, and bulging of the <u>tricuspid valve</u> into the <u>right atrium</u><br><br> | <br>* cv wave : severe <u>tricuspid valve regurgitation</u><br><br> |
| x descent | <br>* A drop in <u>JVP</u> caused by atrial relaxation<br><br> | <br>* Absent in:<br><br>* <u>Tricuspid valve regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Right heart failure</u><br><br> |
| v wave | <br>* The third peak caused by venous refilling of the <u>right atrium</u> against the closed <u>tricuspid valve</u><br><br> | <br>* Prominent in:<br><br>* <u>Tricuspid valve regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Right heart failure</u><br><br> |
| y descent | <br>* A drop in <u>JVP</u> caused by decreased <u>right atrial pressure</u> as blood flows into the <u>right ventricle</u> after opening of the <u>tricuspid valve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Prominent in: [[7]](/library/cXXaC9)<br><br>* <u>Tricuspid valve regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u><br><br>* Absent in:<br><br>* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u><br><br>* <u>Tricuspid valve stenosis</u><br><br><br> |

Jugular venous pressure waveform

![Jugular venous pressure waveform](media/cv117wx7xffg9k6y1k48lpxi.jpg)

## Pulses

A <u>pulse</u> wave is produced by ventricular contraction during <u>systole</u>.




### Approach   [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* Three-finger method: palpation with tips of the 2<sup>nd</sup>, 3<sup>rd</sup>, and 4<sup>th</sup> fingers

* Palpate the <u>common carotid artery</u>, <u>radial artery</u>, <u>abdominal aorta</u>, <u>femoral artery</u>, <u>popliteal artery</u>, <u>tibialis posterior</u> <u>artery</u>, and <u>dorsalis pedis artery</u>.

* The carotid <u>artery</u> <u>pulse</u> should never be palpated at the same time bilaterally. [[8]](/library/xbXED9)

* Risk of compression of vessels → cerebral <u>hypoperfusion</u> → <u>syncope</u>

* Risk of hyperstimulation of the <u>carotid sinus</u> reflex → <u>bradycardia</u>/<u>low blood pressure</u> → cerebral <u>hypoperfusion</u> → <u>syncope</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The thumb of the examiner should never be used to take the <u>pulse</u> because its own strong <u>pulse</u> might be mistaken for the patient's <u>pulse</u>.




![Sites of palpation for pulse measurements](media/scg36r3zdj8paktufp2kljqx.jpg)

Sites of palpation for pulse measurements




### Palpation [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The <u>pulse</u> should be assessed for rate, rhythm, character, volume, the speed of upstroke, and delay.




| Palpation of the arterial <u>pulse</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Pulse</u> characteristics | Description | Possible causes |
| Rate | <br><br>* Bradycardia: < 60 bpm<br><br>* Tachycardia: > 100 bpm<br><br>* See also “<u>Normal vital signs at rest</u>” for all age groups.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Physiological variations<br><br>* <u>Bradyarrhythmias</u><br><br>* <u>Tachyarrhythmias</u><br><br><br> |
| Rhythm | <br>* Regular: interval between individual <u>pulse</u> waves remains consistent<br><br> | <br><br>* Physiological (normal)<br><br>* <u>First-degree AV block</u><br><br>* <u>2:1 AV block</u><br><br>* <u>Atrial flutter</u> with a fixed <u>AV block</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>* Regularly irregular pulse: interval between individual <u>pulse</u> waves varies in a consistent pattern, i.e., there is a pattern to the irregularity<br><br> | <br><br>* Atrial <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrial flutter</u>) with a consistently varying <u>AV block</u><br><br>* <u>Respiratory sinus arrhythmia</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Irregularly irregular pulse: a <u>pulse</u> in which the interval between individual <u>pulse</u> waves varies with no consistent pattern<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u><br><br>* Atrial <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>atrial flutter</u>) with an inconsistently varying <u>AV block</u><br><br>* Ventricular ectopics (<u>premature ventricular contractions</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Pulse deficit: the difference between the <u>pulse</u> rate (measured by <u>cardiac auscultation</u>) and the peripheral <u>pulse</u> rate (obtained by palpating the <u>radial artery</u> for 1 minute)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pulse deficit</u> > 10/min: <u>atrial fibrillation</u><br><br>* <u>Pulse deficit</u> < 10/min: <u>premature ventricular contractions</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy</u> (<u>HOCM</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Pulsus bigeminus: a <u>regularly irregular rhythm</u> in which two heartbeats occur in rapid succession followed by a gap (the usual pattern is: high-volume <u>pulse</u>, low-volume <u>pulse</u>, delay, repeat)<br><br> | <br><br>* Severe <u>left heart failure</u><br><br>* <u>Digoxin toxicity</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Volume (amplitude) <br> | <br><br>* Hyperkinetic pulse (<u>pulsus altus</u>): <u>bounding pulse</u><br><br>* Water hammer pulse<br><br>* <u>Bounding pulse</u> with a rapid upstroke followed by a prompt collapse of the vessel<br><br>* Referred to as <u>Corrigan pulse</u> when present in the carotid <u>artery</u><br><br>* Traube sign: pistol shot-like sounds that are heard over the <u>femoral artery</u> upon compression<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Arterial hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperdynamic circulation</u>: <u>anemia</u>, <u>sepsis</u><br><br>* <u>Patent ductus arteriosus</u><br><br>* <u>Ventricular septal defect</u> (<u>VSD</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* Hypokinetic pulse (<u>pulsus parvus</u>): soft <u>pulse</u> with a low amplitude<br><br> | <br>* <u>Low blood pressure</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Pulsus paradoxus: pathological decrease in the <u>pulse</u> wave amplitude and systolic blood pressure > 10 mm Hg during inspiration <br><br>* Decrease of intrathoracic pressure during inspiration → expansion of vena cava and <u>right atrium</u> → ↑ <u>venous return</u> → ↑ RV filling<br><br>* ↓ <u>Pericardial</u> compliance (e.g., due <u>pericardial</u> rigidity in <u>constrictive pericarditis</u>) → ↑ bowing of the ventricular septum into the <u>left ventricle</u> → ↓ LV ejection volume → ↓ systolic blood pressure<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u><br><br>* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u><br><br>* Severe obstructive <u>airway</u> disease (<u>asthma</u>, <u>COPD</u>)<br><br>* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u><br><br>* <u>Croup</u><br><br>* <u>Tension pneumothorax</u><br><br>* <u>Superior vena cava syndrome</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Reverse pulsus paradoxus: <u>pulse</u> volume increases with inspiration<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>HOCM</u><br><br>* <u>AV dissociation</u><br><br>* Intermittent <u>positive pressure ventilation</u> (<u>IPPV</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* Pulsus alternans: alternation of strong and weak pulses caused by alterations in the <u>stroke volume</u> (<u>cardiac output</u>)<br><br>* Dicrotic pulse: two peaks in the <u>pulse</u> wave occurring in <u>systole</u> and <u>diastole</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Congestive heart failure</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Pulsus bisferiens: a <u>pulse</u> wave with two peaks, i.e., a rapid, short <u>pulse</u> followed by a slower, broader <u>pulse</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>HOCM</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Speed of <u>pulse</u> upstroke (wave contour)<br> | <br>* Fast-rising pulse (<u>pulsus celer</u>): rapid upstroke of the <u>pulse</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br> |
| <br>* Slow-rising pulse (<u>pulsus tardus</u>): delayed <u>peak pressure</u> of the carotid <u>artery</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br> |  |
| Delay | <br>* Radiofemoral delay: a delay in palpation of the femoral arterial <u>pulse</u> when compared with the radial arterial <u>pulse</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Coarctation of the aorta</u><br><br>* Vascular obstruction (<u>atherosclerosis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Aneurysms</u><br><br><br> |










### <u>Auscultation</u> [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* <u>Auscultate</u> over the carotid <u>arteries</u>, <u>abdominal aorta</u>, <u>renal arteries</u>, and <u>femoral arteries</u> to detect bruits, which are vascular <u>murmurs</u> caused by <u>turbulent</u>, nonlaminar blood flow in a vessel.

* Causes of <u>bruits</u>

* AV <u>fistulae</u>

* <u>Arteriovenous malformations</u>

* <u>Aneurysms</u>

* Vascular stenosis

* <u>Hyperdynamic circulation</u>

* E.g., <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>anemia</u>, <u>hyperthyroidism</u>

* May occur physiologically in <u>adolescents</u>

## Chest inspection

### Approach [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The patient is asked to undress from the waist up and the physician evaluates for the following:




* Scars (e.g., <u>heart</u> <u>surgery</u>, pacemakers)

* Chest deformities (e.g., <u>pectus carinatum</u>, <u>pectus excavatum</u>)

* Visible apex beat

* Distended <u>veins</u> (e.g., in <u>SVC obstruction</u>)

* <u>De Musset sign</u>: head bobbing in time with the <u>pulse</u> (seen in <u>aortic regurgitation</u>)

---

## Cardiac palpation

### Apex beat [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The apex beat (apex impulse) is the outermost and lowermost palpable cardiac impulse on the <u>chest wall</u>.




#### Palpation of the apex beat [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* Approach

* Performed in the <u>supine position</u> with the torso elevated to 45°

* The examiner places a flat hand on the cardiac apex to locate the apex beat, and further localizes and assesses the beat by palpating with 2–3 fingers.

* If the apex beat is not initially palpable, the patient should be positioned on the left <u>lateral</u> side and the cardiac apex palpated during expiration.

* Normal findings

* Position: 5<sup>th</sup> left <u>intercostal space</u> in the <u>midclavicular line</u>

* Character: a brief (early systolic) impulse that is felt over an area of 2–3 cm<sup>2</sup>





| <br>Abnormalities of the apex beat [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Abnormality | Etiology |
| Position | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> and downward displacement<br><br> | <br>* <u>Left ventricular</u> enlargement<br><br> |
| <br>* Displacement to the right hemithorax<br><br> | <br>* <u>Dextrocardia</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Lateral</u> displacement<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Right ventricular hypertrophy</u><br><br>* Right <u>tension pneumothorax</u><br><br>* Large right-sided <u>pleural effusion</u><br><br>* <u>Chest wall</u> deformities<br><br><br> |  |
| Character | <br>* Hyperdynamic impulse: a brief, forceful impulse palpable over a diffuse area (> 3 cm<sup>2</sup>)<br><br> | <br><br>* High <u>cardiac output</u> (e.g., <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>, <u>anemia</u>, <u>sepsis</u>, <u>beriberi</u>)<br><br>* <u>Volume overload</u>: <u>aortic regurgitation</u>, <u>mitral regurgitation</u>, <u>VSD</u>, <u>patent ductus arteriosus</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>* Heaving impulse: a prolonged, forceful impulse<br><br> | <br>* Pressure overload: <u>hypertension</u>, <u>HOCM</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Hypodynamic impulse: a weak or absent apex impulse<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Myocardial infarction</u><br><br>* Conditions that impair transmission of the apex impulse to the <u>chest wall</u>: <u>obesity</u>, <u>pericardial effusion</u>, left-sided <u>pleural effusion</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>COPD</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Tapping apex beat: palpable <u>first heart sound</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Mitral stenosis</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Dyskinetic apex beat: uncoordinated impulse over a diffuse area<br><br> | <br>* <u>Left ventricular dysfunction</u>, e.g., <u>anterior myocardial infarction</u><br><br> |  |





### Other impulses [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* Parasternal heave

* A heaving motion felt over the left parasternal area while palpating with the heel of the right hand

* Suggests <u>right ventricular hypertrophy</u>

* Thrills: a palpable <u>heart murmur</u>, usually over the region where the <u>murmur</u> is heard best

* Palpable <u>heart sounds</u>

* Palpate over valve areas (see “<u>Auscultatory locations</u>”).

* A palpable <u>P2</u> suggests <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>.

* Epigastric pulsations

* Visible or palpable pulsations over the epigastric region of the abdomen

* Associated with <u>right ventricular hypertrophy</u> or an <u>abdominal aortic aneurysm</u>

---

## Chest percussion

Although cardiac percussion can provide some information about the size and shape of the <u>heart</u>, it is very unreliable and dependent on the examiner and is thus of limited clinical use.

---

## Cardiac auscultation

### Approach [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* The patient should be in a <u>supine position</u> with the torso elevated to 45°.

* Ask the patient to refrain from speaking while the <u>heart sounds</u> are being assessed.

* The radial <u>pulse</u> should be palpated while <u>auscultation</u> is performed.

* If <u>heart sounds</u> are weakly audible, ask the patient to hold their breath after exhaling.

* Assess the following:

* Location, timing, changes in intensity, and splitting of <u>heart sounds</u>

* Abnormal <u>heart sounds</u>

* <u>Murmurs</u>





### Auscultatory locations [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




| <u>Heart sound</u> <u>auscultation</u> sites |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name of area | Location | Pathology |
| Erb point (cardiology) | <br>* 3<sup>rd</sup> left parasternal <u>intercostal space</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Diastolic</u> <u>murmurs</u>: <u>aortic regurgitation</u>, <u>pulmonic regurgitation</u><br><br>* Systolic <u>murmurs</u>: <u>HOCM</u><br><br><br> |
| Aortic area | <br>* 2<sup>nd</sup> right parasternal <u>intercostal space</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Coarctation of the aorta</u><br><br><br> |
| Pulmonic area | <br>* 2<sup>nd</sup> left parasternal <u>intercostal space</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pulmonary stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Pulmonary regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>ASD</u><br><br><br> |
| Mitral area | <br>* 5<sup>th</sup> left <u>intercostal space</u> in the <u>midclavicular line</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mitral stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Mitral regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Mitral valve prolapse</u> (<u>MVP</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Tricuspid area | <br>* 4<sup>th</sup> left parasternal <u>intercostal space</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tricuspid stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Tricuspid regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>VSD</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> "All Physicians Earn Too Much" (Aortic, Pulmonary, Erb point, Tricuspid, Mitral)

## Heart sounds

### Normal <u>heart sounds</u> [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* The first (<u>S1</u>) and second (<u>S2</u>) <u>heart sounds</u> are physiological sounds heard in all healthy individuals.

* The third (<u>S3</u>) and fourth (<u>S4</u>) <u>heart sounds</u> may be physiological (particularly in young adults, pregnant women, and the elderly) or pathological.





| Normal <u>heart sounds</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sound |  | Origin | Location | Timing |
| First heart sound (<u>S1</u>) |  | <br>* Closure of the <u>mitral valve</u> and <u>tricuspid valve</u><br><br> | <br>* Heard best in the <u>mitral area</u> (cardiac apex)<br><br> | <br><br>* At the onset of <u>systole</u><br><br>* Heard just before the carotid pulsation is felt<br><br><br> |
| Second heart sound (<u>S2</u>) | Aortic component of the second heart sound | <br>* Closure of the <u>aortic valve</u> (louder)<br><br> | <br>* Heard best in the <u>aortic area</u> at the right upper sternal border<br><br> | <br><br>* During the transition from <u>systole</u> to <u>diastole</u><br><br>* Heard immediately after the carotid pulsation<br><br>* See also “<u>Splitting of S2</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| Pulmonary component of the second heart sound | <br>* Closure of the <u>pulmonary valve</u> (softer)<br><br> | <br>* Heard best in the <u>pulmonary region</u><br><br> |  |  |





![Heart sounds (physiological) - Clinical examination | Δ AMBOSS](media/small_60753dca299ac.jpg)

Heart sounds (physiological) - Clinical examination | Δ AMBOSS




### Extra <u>heart sounds</u> [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




| <br>Extra <u>heart sounds</u> (gallops)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sound | Origin | Timing | Occurrence |
| Third heart sound (<u>S3</u>) | <br><br>* Due to rapid <u>ventricular filling</u> and sudden deceleration of blood when the ventricle reaches its elastic limit<br><br>* Heard best with the bell of the stethoscope in the <u>mitral area</u> with the patient in a left <u>lateral</u> position<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Early <u>diastolic</u> sound that is heard immediately after <u>S2</u><br><br>* <u>Ventricular gallop</u>: <u>S1</u> is followed by <u>S2</u> and <u>S3</u> in close succession, resembling the cadence of the word “Kentucky” (Ken: <u>S1</u>, tuc-ky: <u>S2</u>, <u>S3</u>) on <u>auscultation</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Physiological: young individuals (< 40 years of age), athletes, or pregnant women<br><br>* Pathological<br><br>* Chronic <u>mitral regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Heart failure</u><br><br>* <u>Dilated cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Thyrotoxicosis</u><br><br><br> |
| Fourth heart sound (<u>S4</u>) | <br><br>* Due to late <u>diastolic</u> contraction of the <u>atria</u> (atrial kick) against high ventricular pressure<br><br>* Heard best with the bell of the stethoscope in the <u>mitral area</u> with the patient lying in a left <u>lateral</u> position<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Late <u>diastolic</u> (presystolic) sound heard immediately before <u>S1</u><br><br>* <u>S1</u> rapidly follows <u>S4</u>, resembling the cadence of the word “Tennessee” (Ten-nes: <u>S4</u>, <u>S1</u>, see: <u>S2</u>) on <u>auscultation</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Physiological: advanced age<br><br>* Pathological if palpable<br><br>* Ventricular <u>hypertrophy</u> (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u>, <u>cor pulmonale</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ischemic cardiomyopathy</u><br><br>* <u>Acute myocardial infarction</u><br><br><br> |





![S3 Heart Sound (S3 Gallop) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 9](media/small_60755ea6bddc8.jpg)

S3 Heart Sound (S3 Gallop) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 9

![S4 Heart Sound (S4 Gallop) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 10](media/small_60755ec0e52b0.jpg)

S4 Heart Sound (S4 Gallop) - Heart Auscultation - Episode 10




> [!NOTE]
> Gallops that originate from the left side of the <u>heart</u> (the most common) become softer with inspiration, while those that originate from the right side become louder.




### Changes in intensity [[9]](/library/3q0SyS)




Increased or decreased intensity (loudness) of the <u>heart sounds</u> may indicate certain pathologies.




#### S1 intensity




* Loud S1 

* <u>Mitral stenosis</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Hyperdynamic states</u> (e.g., left-to-right shunts )

* Short <u>PR interval</u> (e.g., <u>AVRT</u>)

* Soft S1 

* Severe <u>mitral stenosis</u>

* Conditions that impair the transmission of <u>heart sounds</u> to the <u>chest wall</u>: <u>COPD</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>pericardial effusion</u>, <u>obesity</u>

* <u>LBBB</u>

* Prolonged <u>PR interval</u> (e.g., first-degree <u>heart blocks</u>)

* Variable intensity

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u>

* <u>AV dissociation</u>

* <u>Auscultatory</u> alternans: severe <u>LV failure</u>, large <u>pericardial effusion</u>





#### <u>S2</u> intensity




* Loud A2: <u>arterial hypertension</u>, <u>coarctation of the aorta</u>

* Loud <u>P2</u>: <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> , <u>atrial septal defects</u> [[10]](/library/PVXWuC)





### Splitting of <u>heart sounds</u> [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




If the aortic and pulmonary valves do not close simultaneously, an apparent <u>splitting of S2</u> can be heard upon <u>auscultation</u>.




| Splitting of <u>heart sounds</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type of split |  | Description | Causes |
| Split S1 |  | <br>* Occurs when the closure of the <u>tricuspid valve</u> is delayed (e.g., due to an <u>RBBB</u>), resulting in the sound of <u>tricuspid valve</u> closure heard shortly after <u>mitral valve</u> closure<br><br> | <br><br>* Conduction disorders<br><br>* Hemodynamic cause<br><br><br> |
| Split S2<br> | <br>Physiological split <br> | <br>* The sound of <u>aortic valve</u> closure (A2) precedes the sound of <u>pulmonary valve</u> closure (<u>P2</u>) during inspiration<br><br>* Inspiration → fall in intrathoracic pressure → increase in <u>venous return</u> to the right side of the <u>heart</u> → prolonged <u>right ventricular</u> <u>systole</u> → delayed closure of <u>P2</u><br><br>* Pooling of blood in <u>pulmonary circulation</u> → shortened <u>left ventricular</u> <u>systole</u> → premature A2<br><br> | <br>* Especially pronounced among young individuals<br><br> |
| <br>Wide split  <br> | <br><br>* An exaggerated <u>physiological split</u>, which is more pronounced during inspiration (A2 precedes <u>P2</u>)<br><br>* Caused by any condition that increases <u>right ventricular</u> <u>afterload</u> or decreases <u>left ventricular</u> <u>preload</u><br><br>* Increased <u>right ventricular</u> <u>afterload</u> → prolonged <u>right ventricular</u> <u>systole</u><br><br>* Decreased <u>left ventricular</u> <u>preload</u> → shortened <u>left ventricular</u> <u>systole</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Pulmonary valve stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>RBBB</u><br><br>* <u>Massive pulmonary embolism</u><br><br>* Severe <u>mitral regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Fixed split   <br> | <br><br>* Does not change with respiration and tends to be wide, i.e., the split is also audible during expiration<br><br>* <u>Left-to-right shunt</u> in <u>ASD</u> → RV volume overload → delay in the closure of the <u>pulmonary valve</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Atrial septal defect</u> (<u>ASD</u>)<br><br>* Severe <u>RV failure</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Paradoxical split (<u>reversed split</u>)   <br> | <br>* Audible during expiration but not inspiration<br><br>* Expiration: A2 is heard after <u>P2</u> during expiration due to delayed closure of the <u>aortic valve</u> (split reversal)<br><br>* Inspiration: the closure of the <u>pulmonary valve</u> is also delayed, resulting in A2 and <u>P2</u> occurring simultaneously (i.e., a paradoxical decrease in the split during inspiration)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Left bundle branch block</u><br><br>* <u>HOCM</u> (<u>LV outflow tract obstruction</u>)<br><br>* Early excitation of the <u>right ventricle</u> (e.g., RV pacing, <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| Absent split | <br>* No <u>splitting of S2</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Severe aortic stenosis</u> (geriatric)<br><br>* <u>VSD</u> with <u>Eisenmenger syndrome</u> (pediatric)<br><br><br> |  |

### Additional sounds [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* Clicks are crisp sounds produced by the movement of abnormal valves.

* Other sounds may also be heard, such as an <u>opening snap</u>, <u>pericardial friction rub</u>, <u>pericardial knock</u>.





| Additional sounds on <u>cardiac auscultation</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sound | Origin | Timing | Etiology |  |
| Aortic ejection click | <br><br>* Opening of a stiff <u>aortic valve</u><br><br>* Heard best with the <u>diaphragm</u> of a stethoscope at the <u>aortic region</u> with the patient seated and leaning forward<br><br><br> | <br>* Early systolic sound (immediately after <u>S1</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br> |  |
| Mitral valve prolapse click | <br><br>* <u>Mitral valve prolapse</u> into the left <u>atria</u> during <u>systole</u><br><br>* Heard best with the <u>diaphragm</u> of a stethoscope at the <u>mitral region</u> with the patient in left <u>lateral</u> position<br><br><br> | <br>* Midsystolic sound<br><br> | <br>* <u>Mitral valve prolapse</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Mitral valve</u> opening snap | <br><br>* Opening of a stiff <u>mitral valve</u><br><br>* Heard best with the bell of a stethoscope at the <u>mitral region</u> with the patient in a left <u>lateral</u> position<br><br><br> | <br>* Early <u>diastolic</u> sound (immediately after <u>S2</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Mitral stenosis</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Mechanical valve</u> clicks | <br><br>* <u>S1</u> and <u>S2</u> sound like clicks.<br><br>* Heard best with the <u>diaphragm</u> of a stethoscope<br><br><br> | <br>* Coincides with a normal <u>S1</u> and <u>S2</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Prosthetic valve</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Pericardial friction rub</u> | <br><br>* Scratching sound due to friction between the <u>visceral</u> and <u>parietal pericardium</u><br><br>* Heard best over the left sternal border during expiration with the patient sitting upright and leaning forward<br><br><br> | <br>* Systolic or <u>diastolic</u> sound<br><br> | <br>* <u>Pericarditis</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Pericardial knock</u> | <br><br>* Sudden cessation of <u>ventricular filling</u> against a rigid <u>pericardial</u> sack<br><br>* Heard best at the left sternal border<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Diastolic</u> sound<br><br> | <br>* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> The presence of an aortic <u>ejection click</u> can be used to differentiate a pathological systolic <u>murmur</u> of <u>aortic stenosis</u> from a <u>flow murmur</u>. When the click is present, the <u>murmur</u> is pathological.




> [!TIP]
> The absence of a click in patients with <u>prosthetic valves</u> may indicate valve failure.

## Heart murmurs

### Overview [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* <u>Murmurs</u> are blowing or whooshing sounds that occur as a result of <u>turbulent blood flow</u>.

* They are described according to the location, radiation, timing, intensity, configuration, frequency, and response to dynamic maneuvers.

* For specific <u>auscultatory</u> findings in <u>valvular heart disease</u>, see “<u>Auscultation in valvular defects</u>.”

* For specific <u>auscultatory</u> findings of <u>heart</u> defects, see “<u>Congenital heart defects</u>.”





#### Functional and pathological <u>murmurs</u>




<u>Murmurs</u> may be functional or pathological.




| Difference between functional and pathological <u>murmurs</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Criteria | <br>Functional heart murmur (physiological or innocent) | Pathological <u>murmur</u> |
| Etiology | <br><br>* An ejection <u>murmur</u> due to increased or <u>turbulent blood flow</u> across normal aortic and/or pulmonary valves, e.g., due to a <u>hyperdynamic circulation</u><br><br>* Most commonly occurs in children and young adults<br><br>* Cardiac pathology must be ruled out.<br><br><br> | <br>* Caused by structural defects (valvular disease or <u>heart</u> defects)<br><br> |
| Intensity | <br>* Soft (grade < 3/6 without a <u>thrill</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Typically grade > 3/6<br><br>* <u>Thrill</u> may be present<br><br><br> |
| Timing | <br>* Most commonly midsystolic or continuous<br><br> | <br>* Systolic, <u>diastolic</u>, or continuous<br><br> |
| Position change | <br>* Position-dependent; varies in intensity or disappears<br><br> | <br>* Rarely disappears<br><br> |





### Location and radiation [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




* Location: see “<u>Auscultatory locations</u>.”

* Radiation 

* <u>Aortic stenosis</u>: a systolic <u>murmur</u> radiates to carotid <u>arteries</u>

* <u>Mitral regurgitation</u>: a systolic <u>murmur</u> radiates to the left <u>axilla</u> (in the left <u>lateral</u> <u>recumbent position</u>)

* <u>Pulmonary stenosis</u>: a systolic <u>murmur</u> radiates to the interscapular region





### Timing [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




| <br>Timing of <u>heart murmurs</u> [[11]](/library/IVXYDC) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Murmur</u> | <br>Timing<br> | Occurrence |  |
| Functional | Pathological |  |  |
| <br>Systolic <u>murmur</u>  <br> | <br><br>* During ventricular contraction (i.e., occurs with or after <u>S1</u> and before <u>S2</u>)<br><br>* Can be classified as:<br><br>* Early systolic murmur<br><br>* Midsystolic murmur<br><br>* Late systolic murmur<br><br>* Holosystolic murmur<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Children<br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br>* During states of excitement or strenuous activity<br><br>* <u>Anemia</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u>, <u>sepsis</u><br><br>* <u>Thyrotoxicosis</u><br><br>* <u>Beriberi</u><br><br>* <u>Arteriovenous fistula</u><br><br>* Still murmur<br><br>* Most common <u>innocent murmur</u> in children<br><br>* Grade 1–3 <u>midsystolic murmur</u> heard best at the left midsternal border or between the left lower sternal border and the apex<br><br>* Louder when the patient is <u>supine</u> and softer when the patient is upright<br><br>* Unknown etiology<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Aortic stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Pulmonary stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Mitral regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Tricuspid regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>VSD</u><br><br>* <u>Coarctation of the aorta</u><br><br>* <u>HOCM</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Diastolic</u> <u>murmur</u>  <br> | <br><br>* During ventricular relaxation (i.e., occurs with or after <u>S2</u> and before <u>S1</u>)<br><br>* Can be classified as:<br><br>* Early diastolic murmur<br><br>* Middiastolic murmur<br><br>* Late diastolic murmur<br><br>* Holodiastolic murmur<br><br><br> | <br>* Does not occur physiologically<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mitral stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Tricuspid stenosis</u><br><br>* <u>Pulmonary regurgitation</u><br><br><br> |
| Continuous murmur | <br>* During <u>systole</u> and <u>diastole</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hyperdynamic state</u><br><br>* Cervical venous hum<br><br>* Common benign finding in children due to <u>turbulent flow</u> in <u>internal jugular veins</u><br><br>* Heard best at the infraclavicular and supraclavicular regions (more common on the right side)<br><br>* Becomes softer or disappears with <u>flexion</u> of the head, compression of the jugular <u>vein</u>, or in the <u>supine position</u><br><br>* May radiate to the 1<sup>st</sup> and 2<sup>nd</sup> <u>ICS</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>PDA</u><br><br>* <u>Arteriovenous fistulas</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Diastolic</u> <u>murmurs</u> are almost always pathological.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Diastolic</u> <u>murmurs</u> may require certain maneuvers to make them more apparent, e.g., letting the patient sit and lean forward to intensify the <u>murmur</u> of <u>aortic regurgitation</u>.




### Intensity [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The intensity refers to the loudness of the <u>murmur</u> on <u>auscultation</u> (grades I–VI).




| <br>Grading of <u>murmur</u> intensity [[12]](/library/tVXXwC) |  |
| --- | --- |
| Levine grading scale | Intensity |
| Grade I | <br>* Very faint <u>murmur</u> only heard upon careful <u>auscultation</u><br><br> |
| Grade II | <br>* Faint <u>murmur</u>, but can be detected almost immediately<br><br> |
| Grade III | <br><br>* Easily heard<br><br>* No <u>thrill</u><br><br><br> |
| Grade IV | <br>* Loud <u>murmur</u> with a palpable <u>thrill</u><br><br> |
| Grade V | <br><br>* Very loud <u>murmur</u> with an easily palpable <u>thrill</u><br><br>* Audible with just the rim of the stethoscope touching the chest<br><br><br> |
| Grade VI | <br><br>* Loudest possible <u>murmur</u><br><br>* Audible with the stethoscope hovering above the chest<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> While most grade III and above <u>murmurs</u> are pathological, the intensity of a <u>murmur</u> does not always correlate to the severity of the underlying lesion. For example, a larger <u>VSD</u> produces a softer <u>murmur</u> than a small <u>VSD</u>, and a <u>murmur</u> of <u>severe aortic stenosis</u> may disappear if a patient develops <u>left heart failure</u>.




> [!TIP]
> All <u>diastolic</u> <u>murmurs</u> and any grade II and above systolic <u>murmurs</u> require further <u>echocardiographic</u> evaluation.




### Configuration [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The configuration describes the change in intensity (loudness) of a <u>murmur</u>, which is determined by the pressure gradient driving the <u>turbulent flow</u>.



* Types  

* Uniform: unchanging intensity

* Crescendo: increasing intensity

* Decrescendo: decreasing intensity

* Crescendo-decrescendo: initial increase followed by a decrease in intensity




![Phonocardiogram of systolic heart murmurs](media/wm218fjd3ro96w83qtjiz00e.jpg)

Phonocardiogram of systolic heart murmurs

![Phonocardiogram of diastolic murmurs](media/xvzrw8kmurvuglkkm5sqmg3g.jpg)

Phonocardiogram of diastolic murmurs




### Frequency (pitch) [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




The frequency of a <u>murmur</u> is determined by the <u>velocity</u> of <u>turbulent flow</u>, which is in turn affected by the pressure gradient.




* High pitch: high-pressure gradient and high-<u>velocity</u> flow (e.g., <u>VSD</u>)

* Low pitch: low-pressure gradient and low-<u>velocity</u> flow (e.g., <u>mitral stenosis</u>)





### Maneuvers [[1]](/library/-ZXDV9)




Certain maneuvers may be performed to elicit a change in the intensity of a <u>murmur</u>.




| Maneuvers and their effect on murmurs |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maneuver | Effect on cardiac parameters | Effect on <u>murmurs</u> |  |
| <br>Inspiration <br> | <br><br>* ↑ RV <u>preload</u><br><br>* ↓ LV <u>preload</u><br><br>* No effect on LV <u>afterload</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> arising from the right side of the <u>heart</u><br><br>* ↓ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> arising from the left side of the <u>heart</u> (see “Exceptions to maneuvers” below)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Valsalva maneuver</u>/standing | <br><br>* ↓ RV <u>preload</u><br><br>* ↓ LV <u>preload</u><br><br>* ↓ LV <u>afterload</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Intensity of <u>MVP</u> (with early midsystolic click) and <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u> (<u>HCM</u>) <u>murmurs</u><br><br>* ↓ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> arising from the left side of the <u>heart</u> (see “Exceptions to maneuvers” below)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Squatting/lying down quickly/raising the legs <br> | <br><br>* ↑ RV <u>preload</u><br><br>* ↑ LV <u>preload</u><br><br>* No effect on LV <u>afterload</u> (<u>afterload</u> may increase with squatting)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Intensity of all <u>murmurs</u> (see “Exceptions to maneuvers” below)<br><br>* ↓ Intensity of <u>MVP</u> (with late midsystolic click) and <u>HCM</u> <u>murmurs</u><br><br>* <u>Tetralogy of Fallot</u>: The severity of <u>tet spells</u> and the associated <u>murmurs</u> decrease with squatting.<br><br>* <u>MVP</u>: click occurs later in <u>systole</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Hand grip <br> | <br><br>* No effect on RV <u>preload</u><br><br>* No effect on LV <u>preload</u><br><br>* ↑ LV <u>afterload</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> resulting from backward flow of blood in the left side of the <u>heart</u> (e.g., <u>aortic regurgitation</u>, <u>mitral regurgitation</u>, <u>VSD</u>, <u>MVP</u>)<br><br>* ↓ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> associated with forward flow of blood in the left side of the <u>heart</u> (e.g., <u>mitral stenosis</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u>, <u>HCM</u>)<br><br>* <u>MVP</u>: click occurs later in <u>systole</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Sitting and leaning forward | <br>* No effect<br><br> | <br>* ↑ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> at or near the <u>aortic valve</u> (e.g., <u>aortic stenosis</u>, <u>aortic regurgitation</u>, <u>coarctation of the aorta</u>, <u>HOCM</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Lying down in the left <u>lateral</u> position | <br>* No effect<br><br> | <br>* ↑ Intensity of <u>murmurs</u> at or near the <u>mitral valve</u> (e.g., <u>mitral stenosis</u>, <u>mitral regurgitation</u>, <u>MVP</u>)<br><br> |  |





#### Exceptions to maneuvers




In the following conditions, maneuvers that increase <u>preload</u> decrease the intensity of the <u>murmur</u> and vice versa.




* <u>HOCM</u>

* <u>MVP</u>





> [!TIP]
> Maneuvers that decrease LV <u>preload</u> (e.g., inspiration, <u>Valsalva maneuver</u>) usually decrease the intensity of <u>murmurs</u> arising from the left side of the <u>heart</u>, except in <u>HOCM</u> and <u>MVP</u>, in which a decrease in LV <u>preload</u> increases the intensity of the <u>murmur</u>.

## Diagnostics

### Diagnostic tests [[13]](/library/HMbKJ8)




* Noninvasive imaging

* <u>Electrocardiography</u>

* <u>Chest x-ray (heart)</u>

* <u>Echocardiography</u>

* <u>Cardiac MRI</u>/<u>cardiac CT</u>

* <u>Myocardial perfusion scan</u> (especially for <u>coronary artery disease</u>)

* <u>Cardiac stress testing</u>

* <u>Cardiac catheterization</u> [[13]](/library/HMbKJ8)

* <u>Coronary angiography</u>

* <u>Ventriculography</u>

* <u>Electrophysiological study</u>

* <u>Right heart catheterization</u>

* <u>Myocardial biopsy</u>





### Chest x-ray (heart)




The <u>heart</u> shadow can be viewed on a <u>chest x-ray</u>.




* <u>Heart</u> contour in the <u>lateral</u> view 

* <u>Anterior</u> border: <u>right ventricle</u>

* Inferior border: <u>left ventricle</u>

* Posterosuperior border: <u>left atrium</u>

* <u>Heart</u> contour in the posteroanterior (PA) view  

* Right border (from <u>caudal</u> to <u>cranial</u>): <u>right atrium</u>, <u>superior vena cava</u>

* Left border (from <u>caudal</u> to <u>cranial</u>): <u>left ventricle</u>, <u>left atrial appendage</u>, <u>pulmonary trunk</u>, <u>aortic knuckle</u>

* Inferior border: <u>right ventricle</u>

* Cardiothoracic ratio (<u>heart</u> size)

* The cardiac diameter is divided by the thoracic diameter on the same horizontal level in a PA view.

* The normal <u>cardiothoracic ratio</u> is between 0.42 and 0.5.

* Cardiomegaly: an enlarged <u>heart</u> (<u>cardiothoracic ratio</u> > 0.5) due to a variety of conditions, e.g., <u>arterial hypertension</u>, <u>CAD</u>, <u>athletic heart syndrome</u>

* Assess the <u>lung</u> fields, e.g., for <u>signs of pulmonary edema</u>.
